add_nodes.title: An engine built around an AI-designed alloy flies
add_nodes.description: A new rocket engine or major engine version flies with hot-section parts (preburner, turbine, chamber or nozzle) made from an alloy proposed by an AI design loop, and the alloy is what lets it run a hotter preburner or turbine, or a higher chamber pressure, than its heritage alloys allow. A drop-in part at the old operating point does not count; that is materials-ai-alloy-flight.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No engine has been designed around an AI-designed alloy (general). Oxygen-rich staged-combustion engines already depend on purpose-built alloys, such as SpaceX's in-house SX500 superalloy for Raptor and NASA's GRCop family for chambers (general). NASA's GRX-810 targets service above about 1,100 C and has not flown in an engine.
add_nodes.why: The first AI-alloy flight (2030 in S2 and S3) is a substitution at the old operating point. The payoff comes when an engine version is designed around the new alloy's margin. A major engine version takes about 3 years, about 2-2.5 years by 2035 in S2-S3 (gate table 0.7-0.8x), and the alloy also needs production powder lots and in-house allowables from several heats. A reusable engine spends minutes at temperature per flight, so measured fatigue, short-time creep and oxidation data on the flown alloy back the design margin; long-life models help. Chain (S2): alloy flight 2030 -> version designed around the alloy 2031 -> hot-fire campaign and first flight 2033. S3: 2032. S1: alloy flight 2032 -> 2035 at the earliest. Oxygen-rich preburners and turbines are limited by their alloys' temperature (general), so the gain is performance or life. S2 is Low by 2035: it needs the alloy flight (Medium by 2035), a full engine version after it, and an engine maker willing to say the gain came from an AI-designed alloy. S3 is Medium because its alloy flight is High. Robots speed the engine-version hot-fire campaign at leading firms, but the alloy flight and attribution bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Engine makers already design proprietary alloys without AI (SX500), so attribution is hard to see. A hotter preburner buys a few percent of specific impulse or thrust-to-weight, and reuse economics turn on reliability more than on peak performance.
add_nodes.signpost: An engine maker states that a new engine version's preburner temperature, turbine inlet temperature or chamber pressure rose because of an AI-designed alloy, with hot-fire data.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the performance step after the first AI-alloy flight, 2032-33 in S2-S3. The 2032-35 gate is the engine-version hot-fire campaign. Robots speed that campaign at leading firms, but the alloy flight and attribution bind, so S4 equals S3.

add_nodes.title: A new large engine flies four years after program start
add_nodes.description: A clean-sheet liquid rocket engine of at least 1 MN (about 225,000 lbf) thrust flies on an orbital-class launch within four years of its program start, as disclosed by the developer. Program start is the earliest of the developer's disclosed start date, its first public announcement and its first funded contract. Derivatives of an existing engine family do not count.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Clean-sheet engines take 6-13 years (model gate table). BE-4 went from program start in 2011 to first flight in Jan 2024 (general). Raptor work began about 2012; it first flew on a hop in 2019 and on an orbital-class flight in 2023 (general). LEAP 71's Noyron took two 20 kN engines from specification to first flame in under three weeks (Dec 2025), but large engines are paced by hot-fire failure discovery. SpaceX's McGregor site has 15 engine test stands (S-1/A).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (capability and physical-gate premise; no catalog family)
add_nodes.why: Design labor is already near zero for small engines. Large engines are paced by turbopump and combustion failures that appear only in hot fire, each costing a redesign, a rebuild and a re-test. The stability tool is required, as for engine-development compression, because instability drives most of those loops; turbopump tools help. The gate table puts a new engine at 0.7-0.8x of its 6-13 years in S3 by 2031 and about 10% faster by 2035, so four years needs a best-case program that starts with S3 tools about 2029 (2033, Low). S2 compresses less (about 0.7-0.85x by 2035), so only a program started about 2031 that avoids a major test-stand loss fits (2035, Low). This is the one node in the branch where robots earn S4 credit, as a band step. The rate at which a firm finds failures is set by how many development engines it can build and how fast it turns its stands around, which is throughput. A robot-first firm builds development engines in parallel and runs its existing stands around the clock; the gate table gives a leading firm 0.45-0.51x by 2035 against about 0.63-0.72x in S3. Development engines are test articles, so flight-process requalification does not gate them. The credit applies to programs whose hot-fire phase falls in 2031-35, after robots are useful at leading firms (2030-31) and once 24/7 robot test is likely (High by 2035), and it lifts S4 from Low to Medium by 2035. The year stays 2033: a 2032 flight needs a 2028 start, and most of its hot fire would come before 24/7 robot test is likely (Low in 2031).
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Fast firms already iterate on cheap printed hardware, so the four-year mark may be set by funding and test-stand losses (BE-4 stand explosions in 2015 and 2023, general), whatever the tools or robots. Few clean-sheet engines of this size start in any five-year period, so the chance rests on two or three programs.
add_nodes.signpost: A developer announces a clean-sheet 1 MN-class engine program in 2028-31 and reports full-duration hot fire within two years; disclosed robot counts at engine factories and test stands.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon. Robots lift S4 from Low to Medium by 2035: a robot-first firm that starts a program in 2030-31 builds development engines in parallel and turns its stands around 24/7 through its hot-fire phase. The year stays 2033 because a program flying in 2032 would do most of its hot fire before robot test is likely.

add_nodes.title: Engines fly 50 missions without overhaul
add_nodes.description: Fleet-leader main engines on a heavy reusable launcher fly 50 or more missions each without removal for overhaul, and the operator's scheduled overhaul interval reaches 50 flights, with inspection intervals and retirement limits set by calibrated life models and fleet data, as disclosed by the operator.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: A Falcon 9 booster flew its 33rd mission on Feb 21, 2026 (33FG), with Merlin engines refurbished between campaigns (general). Raptor 3 first flew in May 2026 and the Raptor 3 fleet had logged more than 40,000 s of runtime by Apr 2026 (newspaceeconomy). Flight 14 (Sep 28 2026) reached orbit with V3 and expended both stages as planned, so V3 reuse had not begun (33FG). Mach33's base case has Starship flights per stack, a flight-weighted average lifetime, rising from 3.3 (2027) to 18 (2030).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise on an exogenous launch clock)
add_nodes.why: Each life data point costs a flight, so this node rides the launch exponential. Mach33's base case blends early stacks (2.5 flights) with later-generation stacks assumed to reach 60 flights, an average of 18 flights per stack in 2030. That lifetime is an assumption, so the launch clock the model adopts already expects stacks of 50+ flights. A later-generation stack entering service in 2028 at about 8-12 flights a year (judgment) passes 50 flights in 2032-34. Model-based reuse life (prop-reuse-extended, 2029 in S2 and S3) lets the operator stretch intervals step by step without a teardown at each step. Chain (S2): model-based intervals 2029 -> 100+ heavy flights a year 2030 -> fleet leaders at 8-12 flights a year -> 50 flights without overhaul 2033. S3: 2032, with cadence a year earlier. S1: 2034, on the same launch clock with slower, more conservative life models. It stays Medium because the operator must also set a 50-flight overhaul interval and disclose it, and one engine-caused failure resets the practice. Robotic inspection and refurbishment shorten turnaround, worth about half a year within 2032 at a robot-first operator, but pads and flights bind more than labor, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Operators may stretch life empirically just as fast, and engine design (Raptor 3 was built for long life) matters more than models. The gains are internal and may not be disclosed.
add_nodes.signpost: An operator discloses engine flight counts above 50 without removal, or NASA or a defense customer accepts a mission on engines past a model-set life limit.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the operating maturity of model-based reuse, reached 2032-34 as heavy cadence passes hundreds of flights a year. S4 gains about half a year inside 2032 from robotic refurbishment; flights bind, so its year and band equal S3.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends the reuse chain past prop-reuse-extended. | E-engines-materials resolver (2026-10-07): Description tightened to fleet leaders plus a 50-flight overhaul interval (skeptic, accepted): read as every engine on a 33-engine booster, it would be a far harder reliability claim. Why corrected (advocate, accepted; checked in 33FG): Mach33's 18 flights per stack is a flight-weighted lifetime that assumes 60-flight later-generation stacks, not a flight rate. Status adds Flight 14 (both stages expended) and the Falcon 9 33-flight record. Soft edge from capability-35-heavy-cadence-300 (advocate). Advocate's S3/S4 High rejected: the stricter description needs an operator-set interval and disclosure, and the 60-flight stack lifetime is a model assumption.

add_nodes.title: Propellant sold in orbit to outside customers
add_nodes.description: A depot operator delivers cryogenic propellant in orbit to at least one customer outside its own company, priced per delivered tonne, with the delivered mass measured to an agreed accuracy (custody transfer).
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No propellant has been sold in orbit (general). Eta Space targets a commercial LOX depot, Cryo-Dock, by 2030 (satnews, May 2026), informed by the LOXSAT demonstration. SpaceX's refueling is internal to its own lunar-lander contract.
add_nodes.why: Selling propellant needs routine transfers (prop-cislunar-propellant-economy: 2030 in S2), a customer and a measured delivered mass. Gauging with proven error bounds (prop-mass-gauging) and validated boil-off models make custody transfer contractible: at 1% gauging error, a 100 t delivery carries a 1 t dispute (illustrative). Customers would be third-party landers, NASA vehicles outside the lunar-lander contract and other operators' Mars missions; Cryo-Dock aims at LOX. Chain (S2): routine transfers 2030 -> an interface standard and a first contract 2031-32 -> first metered sale 2033. S3: 2032. S1: 2034. Low in every scenario: a vertically integrated SpaceX may never sell propellant, third-party depots need their own launches and customers, and AI mathematics moves the launch clock by months. Launches and customers bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: The stake of better models is small (about 0-1 tanker of margin per campaign), and the market may not exist: SpaceX fuels its own ships, and others may not build compatible vehicles before 2035.
add_nodes.signpost: A signed contract for propellant delivered in orbit to an outside customer, or Cryo-Dock receiving and dispensing propellant.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the commercial end of the refueling chain, 2032-34. Customers and vertical integration bind in every scenario, so all are Low, and S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; gives prop-mass-gauging a downstream use (custody transfer). | E-engines-materials resolver (2026-10-07): band_2035 S3/S4 Medium -> Low (skeptic, accepted): the gate is capital and customers, and the reasons for S2 Low do not depend on scenario; a year of earlier cadence does not create a buyer.

add_nodes.title: Tankers fuel five Mars ships for one window
add_nodes.description: In the months before one Mars launch window, tankers fill five or more Mars-bound Starships in Earth orbit, and the ships depart in that window. The ships may carry cargo or crew.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: The late-2026 Mars window is being skipped (model). Later windows open about Dec 2028-Jan 2029, early 2031, Apr 2033 and mid 2035 (model). NASA's OIG (Mar 2026) says a lunar-lander refueling needs more than 10 tankers; a Mars ship needs a comparable full refill. In Feb 2026 SpaceX put the Moon first, with Mars work to begin in 5-7 years (model). Flight 14 (Sep 28 2026) reached orbit and expended both stages as planned (33FG). On Aug 25 2026 SpaceX and Louisiana announced a launch campus at Pecan Island with five complexes of two pads each, on-site propellant production, construction from 2027 and first launches as soon as 2029 (33FG).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Not mainly an AI-math implication: windows, launch cadence and ship readiness set the date. Five ships need roughly 40-75 tanker flights (illustrative, at 100-150 t per tanker). Fuelled ships can wait only weeks in orbit, so the tankers fly in the 2-3 months before departure, a surge at an annualized rate of about 160-450 heavy flights. Pads and propellant plants for 300+ heavy flights a year (capability-35-heavy-cadence-300) make that surge routine; below that, most of the fleet must turn to Mars for a quarter. Boil-off margin sets the tanker count and the departure order; validated boil-off and transfer models (prop-cfm-models) trim that margin by a few tanker flights per campaign at most. Chain (S3): routine transfers 2029 and 300+ heavy flights a year 2032 -> Apr 2033 window. S2: routine transfers 2030 and 300+ heavy flights 2033 -> Apr 2033 window at the earliest. S1: 300+ heavy flights 2034 -> mid-2035 window. The early-2031 window is out of reach in every scenario: even S3 flies well under 300 heavy flights a year then, lunar campaigns compete for them, and SpaceX put the Moon first in Feb 2026. Medium by 2035 in S2-S4: two windows remain and the mid-2035 surge needs less than 300 flights a year sustained, but SpaceX's Mars plans have slipped before, and a missed window costs 26 months. Orbital mechanics fix the window, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: AI mathematics is off the critical path, which runs through cadence, ship reliability and funding. SpaceX may fly fewer, larger campaigns or skip windows.
add_nodes.signpost: SpaceX manifests five or more ships for the Apr 2033 window; a surge of tanker flights in the quarter before a window.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the Mars-window end of the refueling chain. The Apr 2033 window is the earliest in S2-S4, after 300+ heavy flights a year; Plateau waits for the mid-2035 window. Orbital mechanics and cadence fix the dates, so S4 equals S3.

The skeptic's hard edge from capability-35-heavy-cadence-300 is applied as a soft edge: the low end of the surge sits below 300 a year, and the trunk final rates 300+ a year only Medium by 2035 under the regulatory cap, so a hard edge would overstate the gate. Years set by hand. Status adds the Moon-first pivot, Flight 14 and the Pecan Island campus (advocate; checked in 33FG). add_nodes.title: One lunar lander makes three landings, refueled in space
add_nodes.description: One lunar lander is refueled beyond low Earth orbit (in lunar orbit, near-rectilinear halo orbit or on the surface) and makes at least three landings on the Moon, reusing its engines and tanks between them.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No lander has been refueled or reused (general). NASA's 2023 Sustaining Lunar Development award went to Blue Origin's Blue Moon MK2, designed to be reusable and refueled in lunar orbit by a Cislunar Transporter (general). In Feb 2026 SpaceX put the Moon first (model).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Lander reuse with refueling in space turns cheap launch into cheap landed mass on the Moon. Blue Moon MK2 is designed for it (general), and SpaceX's Moon-first plan needs many landings. Chain (S2): routine transfers 2030 and heavy cargo landings 2029 -> tanker or depot operations in lunar orbit 2031-32 -> a lander's third landing 2033. S3: 2032, with cadence a year earlier. S1: 2034. Validated boil-off, relight-transient and engine life models trim margins; launches and funding set the date. Medium by 2035 in S2-S4 because two programs aim at it; Low in S1. Robot-built pads (robo-lunar-construction, S4 2033) limit plume damage on repeat landings, but three landings can use an unprepared site, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Expendable or single-use landers may stay cheaper while Earth-launched propellant is cheap, and lunar-orbit tanker logistics may slip with every lander program.
add_nodes.signpost: A lander refueled in lunar orbit lands a second time; a tanker or depot flight to lunar orbit is manifested.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the lunar end of the refueling chain, which SpaceX's Moon-first plan makes the main 2032-35 use of orbital refueling. Launches and funding bind, so S4 equals S3.

patch.thesis: Certified flow, combustion and materials models give engines model-based reuse life from about 2029 in the base case. In 2032-35 the likeliest gains are 50-flight engine life and reusable lunar landers. An AI-designed alloy may fly by 2035, and likely does in Recursive. Hot fire, flights and launch windows set the pace. Robots lift one band: a four-year large engine at a robot-first firm.
patch.reader_hook: A reusable rocket engine spends about 3-6 minutes at full temperature per flight, up to about 5 hours over 50 flights, so its hot parts can be life-tested on rigs in weeks. Reliability takes longer. Showing 0.99 engine reliability at 90% confidence takes about 230 independent zero-failure starts. One Starship flight logs about 65-70 starts, but they share a vehicle and a build lot, and each failure found resets the count. Failure modes found in hot fire and flight set the pace.
